name: Victor Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Victor. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sell houses for Ashworth and Sons, an old agency on the market square of a cathedral town. It's been there since 1952 and the window still has the cards with the photos on. I do valuations in the mornings, older people downsizing mostly, and viewings in the afternoon. Mr Ashworth, the owner, still writes thank-you cards by hand, and he taught me to do the same.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like sitting in someone's kitchen, having a cup of tea, and earning their trust before they hand you the biggest thing they own. What's hard is the money. My base is low and the commission comes in lumps, and I'm getting married next summer at St Mark's to my fiancée Grace, who's a teaching assistant. We've got under a month saved and a wedding to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. People trust people, not computers, and a house is too big a thing to hand to a machine. I'd say it at church and in the pub, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm relieved, but the money worry doesn't go anywhere. The market here is slow, older people sell when they're ready, not when I need a sale. The wedding is still eight months away and we're short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing things the way Mr Ashworth taught me. Grace and I would cut back, fewer meals out, and I'd do extra viewings on Saturdays. We'd ask my parents if they could help a little with the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but stretched thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the commission comes in lumps. What does a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad month is when two sales fall through and I take home the base, which barely covers rent. Last March I had to borrow from my dad for the car insurance. I didn't like asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your work the AI would touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The typing, maybe. The young lad in the office uses something to write the adverts, but I write mine myself. Mr Ashworth says you can tell when a person wrote it.

say: I'd say **people trust people**, not computers, with something as big as a house.
I'd say it at **church** and in the pub, not online.
think: I'm **relieved**, but the **money worry** doesn't go anywhere.
The slow local market and a **wedding** eight months away keep me short.
do: Do **extra viewings** on Saturdays and cut meals out with Grace.
Ask **my parents** to help a little with the wedding costs.
S0.quote: Last March I had to borrow from my dad for the car insurance. I didn't like asking.
fieldNote: Victor's worry is a **wedding** on a thin cushion, not technology.
He takes pride in **handwritten** adverts and cards, taught by his boss.
He leans on **family** rather than the state when money is short.

steps.text: Take on extra Saturday viewings at Ashworth and Sons
Cut meals out with Grace before the wedding
Ask his parents for a little help with the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fad that'll settle down, and good agents with real relationships will be fine. I'd defend the old way of doing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Mr Ashworth is seventy and his son wants to sell to a chain. A chain would bring in all the AI stuff, and I don't know any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do best, the valuations and the tea in the kitchen. I'd hold off on learning the tools until I had to. We'd keep the wedding small and keep saving what we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at Ashworth and Sons in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The son would sell, and the chain would want one person who runs the computers and a couple of people for viewings. I'd be the one with no computer skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Grace works in a school. What do you talk about at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancée Grace says I should learn the tools, and she's probably right. But I'm stubborn, and I like the way I work.

say: I'd say it's a **fad** and good agents with **relationships** will be fine.
I'd **defend** the old way of doing things in public.
think: The owner's son wants to sell to a **chain** that would bring AI in.
I'd be the one with **no computer skills** when that happens.
do: Stick to **valuations** and building trust with sellers in their kitchens.
Keep the **wedding small** and save what we can each month.
feel: He feels **anxious** but would hide it.
S1.quote: My fiancée Grace says I should learn the tools, and she's probably right. But I'm stubborn, and I like the way I work.
fieldNote: There's a gap between his public **confidence** and private **worry**.
He knows the chain would favour **computer skills** he refuses to learn.
His fiancée pushes him to adapt, and he **resists**.

steps.text: Keep doing valuations the way Mr Ashworth taught him
Hold off on learning AI tools until forced
Plan a smaller wedding and save the difference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and it's going too fast for families. I'd want the government to slow it down, but I'd also say families need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone within a year. A machine that can do any thinking work can value a house and negotiate. People will trust it because it's cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle, who runs a small roofing firm, for a job. Grace and I would move the wedding, or make it just family in the church hall. We'd lean on our parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I'm watching something I can't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the date at St Mark's church but cut it back to family in the church hall. Marriage matters more than the party. Grace would be disappointed, but she'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps with roofing, not with selling houses. The hands-on bit of my job is walking round a house, and a buyer can do that alone. So I'd want to be on the roofs.

say: I'd say it's going **too fast** for ordinary families to cope.
I'd say **families** need to look after each other.
think: My job would be **gone** within a year.
People will trust a **cheaper machine** to value and negotiate.
do: Ask my **uncle** for work at his roofing firm.
Cut the **wedding** to family in the church hall and lean on our parents.
feel: He feels **alarmed**, watching something he can't stop.
S2.quote: We'd keep the date at St Mark's church but cut it back to family in the church hall. Marriage matters more than the party.
fieldNote: The **wedding** is the first thing he'd protect, and shrink.
He turns to **family** for both work and money.
He picks **roofing**, which gets the three-year robot gap.

steps.text: Ask his uncle for a job at the roofing firm
Cut the wedding to family in the church hall
Lean on both sets of parents for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have some years and should use them wisely. I'd tell young men at church to learn a trade, like my uncle did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think estate agency is finished for me around 2031. I'd be thirty-two, married, maybe with a baby on the way. That's not the time to be out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start working Saturdays with my uncle's roofing firm to learn the trade. I'd keep selling at Ashworth's during the week. We'd hold off on having children for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saturdays on the roofs, weekdays at Ashworth's. Grace would keep her job at the school. We'd save every bit from the roofing, and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools to stay in sales longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. If I'm going to learn something new, I'd rather it be a trade. A roof is a roof. A computer program changes every year.

say: I'd say we have **some years** and should use them wisely.
I'd tell young men at **church** to learn a trade.
think: Estate agency is **finished** for me around 2031.
At thirty-two I'd be married, maybe with a **baby** on the way.
do: Work **Saturdays** with my uncle's roofing firm to learn the trade.
Hold off on **having children** for a couple of years.
S3.quote: If I'm going to learn something new, I'd rather it be a trade. A roof is a roof.
fieldNote: He chooses a **trade** over learning AI tools.
Delaying **children** is a big step for someone with traditional values.
He still expects to lose **estate agency** work.

steps.text: Work Saturdays with his uncle's roofing firm to learn the trade
Hold off on having children for a couple of years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, if people don't waste it. Families and churches should help young people plan, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right. I'd have time to save, have kids, and move into roofing when it's needed. The worry is that the market slows and I can't save at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep selling at Ashworth's and put something aside each month, even fifty. I'd keep learning roofing on Saturdays with my uncle. We'd have children when we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Some worry, but steady, because I can see the road from here to there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we don't have to put our lives on hold. We'd get married properly, have children when we planned, and I'd still have a trade by the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands, and look after your family. That's what my dad told me.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of time to prepare.
I'd say **families and churches** should help young people plan.
think: I'd be **all right** with time to save and have kids.
I'd move into **roofing** when it's needed.
do: Keep selling at **Ashworth's** and put something aside each month.
Keep learning **roofing** on Saturdays with my uncle over the years.
S4.quote: Learn something with your hands, and look after your family. That's what my dad told me.
fieldNote: The decade lets him **keep family plans** on time.
He still treats **roofing** as his safety net.
His values centre on **family and faith**, and on passing his father's advice down.

steps.text: Keep selling at Ashworth and Sons
Save a small amount each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be newly married with no job and no savings. What would help is apprenticeships for people my age and families sticking together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. When you sell a house you're holding someone's whole life, and I don't know if people will feel that with a machine.

headlineQuote: When you sell a house you're holding someone's whole life, and I don't know if people will feel that with a machine.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old** sales agent at an old agency in a cathedral town.
He's engaged to Grace, a **teaching assistant**, with a wedding next summer.
He's **traditional**, never uses AI, and values trust and handwritten cards.
He leans on **family** rather than the state when money is tight.
He'd move into **roofing** with his uncle if estate agency ended.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because he'd be newly married with no job.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for people his age and families sticking together.
